A database layer is only as fast as your slowest queries. This post covers caching strategies: in-memory Redis, TTL management, cache invalidation patterns (TTL, event-driven, LRU), and cache-aside vs write-through patterns.

The most expensive query is the one that runs every time. Let's cache it.

The Caching Problem

Real database query times without cache:

  • User profile lookup: 5ms (database I/O)
  • Leaderboard query: 50ms (sorting 1M records)
  • Product search: 100ms (full-text index scan)
  • Session validation: 2ms (cache miss)

At 10K req/sec, that's:

10,000 req/sec × 5ms = 50 seconds of database CPU/sec
(50 cores fully busy, still can't keep up)

With caching (cache hit rate 90%):

9,000 req/sec (cache hits) → 0.1ms (memory lookup)
1,000 req/sec (cache miss) → 5ms (database)

Component 1: Redis Architecture

Why Redis?

Single-threaded, in-memory, handles 100K ops/sec per core.

Options:
- Memcached: Simple key-value (no expiry, no types)
- Redis: Rich data types (strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams)
- DynamoDB: Managed, expensive ($0.003 per read unit)
- Local memory: No persistence, no sharing across servers

Choice: Redis (Pareto optimal for 90% of use cases)

Redis Data Structures Used

1. Strings (User profiles)
   SET user:123 '{"name":"Alice","score":950}'
   GET user:123 → 0.1ms

2. Hashes (Session data)
   HSET session:abc123 user_id 123 roles "admin,user" token "eyJ..."
   HGET session:abc123 user_id → 0.1ms

3. Sorted Sets (Leaderboards)
   ZADD leaderboard:game1 950 user:123
   ZRANGE leaderboard:game1 0 99 WITHSCORES → 0.5ms (top 100)

4. Lists (Job queues)
   LPUSH jobs:processing job_id_456
   RPOP jobs:processing → 0.2ms

5. Sets (Unique visitors per day)
   SADD visitors:2026-03-27 user:123
   SCARD visitors:2026-03-27 → unique count

Component 2: TTL (Time-To-Live) Management

Problem: How long should data stay cached?

Too short (1 second):

User:123 profile changes
  → Cache expires after 1 sec
  → Next request hits database (cache miss every second)
  → Database load = unoptimized

Real example: Stock price at 100 req/sec, 1-sec TTL
  → 100 requests per second × 10-20ms database → 1 CPU core busy
  → 1 second TTL = cache miss 100% of the time if data changes frequently

Too long (1 hour):

User profile cached for 1 hour
  → User updates name
  → Old name served to 60% of users for 3600 seconds
  → Data inconsistency (bad for banking/payments!)

Right TTL strategy:

Data type             │ TTL  │ Reasoning
─────────────────────┼──────┼─────────────────────
User profile          │ 5m   │ Changes infrequently
Session token         │ 1h   │ Security: short-lived
Leaderboard score     │ 1m   │ Changes frequently
Product catalog       │ 1h   │ Updated via admin UI
Search index          │ 30m  │ Indexed, rebuilt daily
API rate limit quota  │ 1s   │ Per-second counter
Config values         │ 5m   │ Hot reload tolerance

Component 3: Cache Invalidation Patterns

Pattern 1: TTL (Time-based)

// Set with 5-minute expiry
redis.SET(key, value, EX: 300)

// Simple but has stale data problem
// Data stale for up to 5 minutes

Pattern 2: Event-Driven (Invalidate on change)

// User updates profile
POST /api/user/123/profile {name: "Bob"}
  → 1. Update database
  → 2. redis.DEL("user:123")  // Invalidate cache
  → 3. Return response

// Next GET automatically cache-miss → fetches fresh data

Pros: Always fresh
Cons: Must remember to invalidate everywhere

Pattern 3: LRU (Least Recently Used)

// Cache memory limit: 1GB
// When full, evict least recently used entry

Redis config: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

Behavior:
- 1000 keys in cache, 1KB each = 1MB (OK)
- 1M keys = 1GB (at limit)
- Insert new key?
  → Evict least recently used entry
  → Insert new key

Pattern 4: Write-Through Cache

// Update hits both cache and database

func updateUserProfile(userID, name) {
  // 1. Update cache first
  redis.SET("user:" + userID, {name})
  
  // 2. Update database
  db.UPDATE("users SET name = ? WHERE id = ?", userID)
  
  // 3. If DB fails, cache has stale data!
  // (Rollback cache if DB fails)
}

Pros: Writes are fast (1ms to cache)
Cons: Complex error handling (cache/DB mismatch)

Pattern 5: Cache-Aside (Recommended)

// Read logic:
func getUser(userID) {
  // 1. Try cache first
  cached = redis.GET("user:" + userID)
  if cached != nil {
    return cached  // Cache hit
  }
  
  // 2. Cache miss, fetch from DB
  user = db.SELECT("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", userID)
  
  // 3. Store in cache for next time
  redis.SET("user:" + userID, user, EX: 300)
  return user
}

// Write logic:
func updateUser(userID, name) {
  // 1. Update database
  db.UPDATE("users SET name = ? WHERE id = ?", userID)
  
  // 2. Invalidate cache (next read will refetch)
  redis.DEL("user:" + userID)
}

Pros: Simple, no stale data, database is source of truth
Cons: First read after invalidation is slow (cache miss)

Component 4: Cache Hit Rate Monitoring

Measuring cache effectiveness:

Hit rate = (cache hits) / (cache hits + cache misses)

Example:
- 9,000 hits per second
- 1,000 misses per second
- Hit rate = 9,000 / 10,000 = 90%

Performance impact:
- 90% hit rate, 0.1ms hit + 5ms miss
  → Avg latency = 0.9 × 0.1 + 0.1 × 5 = 0.59ms

- 80% hit rate
  → Avg latency = 0.8 × 0.1 + 0.2 × 5 = 1.08ms

- 50% hit rate
  → Avg latency = 0.5 × 0.1 + 0.5 × 5 = 2.55ms

Target: >90% hit rate (diminishing returns above that)

Monitoring in code:

type CacheStats struct {
  Hits      uint64
  Misses    uint64
  Evictions uint64
}

func (stats *CacheStats) hitRate() float64 {
  total := stats.Hits + stats.Misses
  if total == 0 {
    return 0.0
  }
  return float64(stats.Hits) / float64(total)
}

// Update stats on every operation
func (c *Cache) Get(key string) (Value, bool) {
  if val, ok := c.cache[key]; ok {
    atomic.AddUint64(&c.stats.Hits, 1)
    return val, true
  }
  
  atomic.AddUint64(&c.stats.Misses, 1)
  return nil, false
}

Component 5: Cache Stampede Prevention

Problem: Thundering Herd

Time: 13:00:00
- 100 users request user:123 (cache hit)
- Cache entry expires (TTL = 60 seconds)

Time: 13:01:00 (cache expire)
- User A: Cache miss → hits database
- User B: Cache miss → hits database (same query!)
- User C: Cache miss → hits database
- ... 10K concurrent requests all hit database simultaneously

Result: Database slammed, all requests slow down

Solution 1: Probabilistic TTL (Random expiry)

// Don't expire all entries at same time
// Randomize TTL between 270-330 seconds instead of exactly 300s

expiry = 300 + random(0, 60)  // 300-360 seconds
redis.SET(key, value, EX: expiry)

Solution 2: Stale-While-Revalidate

// Cache with two TTLs: soft and hard

soft_ttl = 5 minutes   (stale, but can serve)
hard_ttl = 10 minutes  (expired, must refetch)

func get(key) {
  val, ttl = redis.GET(key)
  
  if ttl > soft_ttl {
    return val  // Fresh
  }
  
  if ttl > 0 {
    // Stale but valid, return value
    // Background: refetch and update cache
    background_refresh(key)
    return val
  }
  
  // Hard expired, must fetch
  val = database_fetch(key)
  redis.SET(key, val)
  return val
}

Complete Caching Layer

┌──────────────────────────┐
│   API Request (50K/sec)   │
└────────────┬─────────────┘
             │
┌────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Cache Layer (Redis)      │
│  Hit rate: 90%            │
└────────────┬──────────────┘
             │ (10% miss)
┌────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Database Query           │
│  Response: 5ms (avg)      │
└────────────┬──────────────┘
             │
┌────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Store in Redis           │
│  TTL: Based on data type  │
└──────────────────────────┘

Performance:
- Cache hit: 0.1ms (memory)
- Cache miss: 5.1ms (DB + store)
- Avg: 0.9 × 0.1 + 0.1 × 5.1 = 0.60ms
- Overall throughput: 50K req/sec sustained

Testing: 30+ Test Cases

✓ Test: GET returns value within TTL
✓ Test: GET returns nil after expiry
✓ Test: SET updates value
✓ Test: DEL removes key
✓ Test: Hit rate calculation accurate
✓ Test: LRU eviction under memory pressure
✓ Test: Event-driven invalidation
✓ Test: TTL randomization prevents stampede
✓ Test: Concurrent reads (race-free)
✓ Test: Cache-aside pattern correctness
✓ Test: Stale-while-revalidate behavior
✓ Test: Redis connection pooling
✓ Test: Fallback if Redis unavailable
✓ Test: Cache key serialization

Real-World Example: E-commerce Site

Product catalog (1M products, 50GB database)
- Each product view hits database → slow

With caching strategy:
1. User searches "shoes"
   → Cache key: "search:shoes"
   → Miss (first request)
   → Query database (100ms, 500 results)
   → Store in cache for 1 hour
   → Return results (100ms)

2. Next 10K searches for "shoes" in same hour
   → Cache hits (all 10,000!)
   → Each returns in 0.1ms
   → Total database CPU: 1 second for first query + 0.1s for monitoring = huge savings

Performance:
- Without cache: 10,000 × 100ms = 1,000 seconds CPU
- With cache: 100ms + 10,000 × 0.1ms = 1.1 seconds CPU
- Improvement: 900x faster

Lessons Learned

1. Cache-aside pattern is safest

Simplest to reason about: database is source of truth, cache is optimization.

2. 90% hit rate is your target

Anything above that has diminishing returns. Below that, you're still hitting the database frequently.

3. TTL matters more than cache size

5-minute TTL on 100K keys beats 1-hour TTL on 1M keys. Quality over quantity.

4. Event-driven invalidation is complex

Easy to forget to invalidate somewhere. Better to rely on TTL + stale-while-revalidate.

5. Redis is the default for good reason

Handles 90% of caching use cases. Predictable performance, rich data types, easy to monitor.

Next: Async Processing & Message Queues

Now that data is cached, we need to handle long-running tasks asynchronously:

  • Background job processing
  • Message queues (RabbitMQ/Kafka)
  • Event-driven architecture
  • Retry policies & dead-letter queues
  • Distributed tracing for async jobs

Some tasks take too long to complete synchronously (sending emails, processing videos, generating reports). This post covers background job processing, message queues (RabbitMQ/Kafka), event-driven architecture, retry policies, and distributed tracing.

The user shouldn't wait for a 10-second email send. Fire-and-forget it.

The Async Problem

Synchronous approach (blocking):

User POST /api/account/register {email, password}
  → 1. Create user in DB (10ms)
  → 2. Send verification email (5000ms) ← BLOCKS!
  → 3. Return response (5010ms)

At 100 req/sec:
  → 100 reqs × 5000ms blocking = 500 seconds CPU time
  → Need 500 cores just for email sending!

Asynchronous approach (fire-and-forget):

User POST /api/account/register {email, password}
  → 1. Create user in DB (10ms)
  → 2. Queue job: {type: "send_email", email, token}
  → 3. Return response immediately (15ms)

Worker processes emails in background:
  → 4. Pop job from queue
  → 5. Send email (5000ms)
  → 6. Mark job as complete

Result: User gets 15ms response, email happens in background

Component 1: Job Queue Architecture

Basic queue:

                 API Server
                     │
                 (enqueue job)
                     ↓
         ┌──────────────────────┐
         │   Job Queue (Redis)  │
         │  [job1, job2, job3]  │
         └──────────────────────┘
                     ↑
            (dequeue job)
                     │
          ┌──────────────────┐
          │  Worker 1        │
          │  Worker 2        │
          │  Worker 3 (pool) │
          └──────────────────┘

Job structure:

{
  id: "job_12345",
  type: "send_email",
  priority: "high",
  payload: {
    email: "user@example.com",
    subject: "Verify your account",
    body: "Click here: ...",
    token: "abc123"
  },
  retries: 0,
  max_retries: 3,
  created_at: "2026-03-27T10:00:00Z",
  scheduled_at: "2026-03-27T10:00:00Z"
}

Component 2: Message Queue Patterns

Pattern 1: Fire-and-Forget (Redis/Resque)

Benefits:
  ✓ Simple: LPUSH job to queue
  ✓ Fast: Enqueue takes 1ms
  ✓ No persistence needed for retries

Limitations:
  ✗ No delivery guarantee (queue crashes = lost jobs)
  ✗ No ordering (jobs may process out of order)

Pattern 2: RabbitMQ (Reliable Queuing)

Benefits:
  ✓ Persistent: Messages written to disk before ACK
  ✓ Durable: Survives broker restart
  ✓ Routing: Messages routed by exchange rules

Process:
  1. Producer sends message
  2. RabbitMQ writes to disk
  3. Returns ACK to producer
  4. Consumer receives message
  5. Consumer processes + sends ACK
  6. RabbitMQ deletes message

Pattern 3: Kafka (Distributed Streaming)

Benefits:
  ✓ Massive scale: 1M messages/sec per broker
  ✓ Replay-able: Messages kept for 7 days
  ✓ Multiple consumers: Many apps read same messages

Use case:
  - Analytics (process millions of events)
  - Logging (centralized event stream)
  - Event replay (re-process historical events)

Component 3: Job Processing

Simple worker loop:

func worker() {
  for {
    // 1. Wait for job (block until available)
    job := queue.BLPop(timeout: 10s)
    if job == nil {
      continue
    }

    // 2. Execute job
    success := processJob(job)

    // 3. Handle result
    if success {
      // Mark as complete (remove from queue)
      continue
    } else {
      // Retry: push back to queue
      if job.retries < job.max_retries {
        job.retries++
        queue.LPUSH(job)
      } else {
        // Dead-letter: move to failed queue
        dead_letter_queue.LPUSH(job)
        logging.Error("Job failed after retries:", job.id)
      }
    }
  }
}

Worker pool (3 workers):

// Start 3 independent workers
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
  go worker()
}

// Now processing 3 jobs in parallel
// Throughput: ~60 emails/sec (if 20ms per email)

Component 4: Retry Policies

Problem: Transient failures (network timeout, service down)

Exponential backoff:

Retry 1: Wait 1 second, try again
Retry 2: Wait 2 seconds, try again
Retry 3: Wait 4 seconds, try again
Retry 4: Wait 8 seconds, try again
Retry 5: Wait 16 seconds, try again

After 5 retries: (1+2+4+8+16) = 31 seconds total

Result: Transient failures auto-recover within 31 seconds
Permanent failures fail fast after 5 attempts

Implementation:

func processJobWithRetry(job Job) bool {
  backoff := 1 // second

  for attempts := 0; attempts <= job.max_retries; attempts++ {
    // Try to process
    err := sendEmail(job.payload)

    if err == nil {
      return true  // Success!
    }

    if attempts < job.max_retries {
      // Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...
      time.Sleep(time.Duration(backoff) * time.Second)
      backoff *= 2
    }
  }

  return false  // All retries exhausted
}

Component 5: Dead-Letter Queues

Problem: Job fails after all retries, what happens?

Solution: Dead-letter queue (DLQ)

                Normal Queue
                     │
    ┌────────────┬────┴────┬──────────────┐
    │            │         │              │
  Success    Temporary   Permanent      MAX_RETRIES
             Failure     Failure        Exceeded
    │            │         │              │
    ↓            ↓         ↓              ↓
 Delete      Retry      Dead-Letter   Dead-Letter
             (backoff)    Queue         Queue

Process:
1. Job fails permanently
2. Retries exhausted
3. Move to DLQ
4. Alert operator
5. Manual investigation

Later:
6. Fix root cause
7. Reprocess DLQ jobs

Component 6: Distributed Tracing for Async Jobs

Problem: Job fails in background, how do we debug?

Trace ID propagation:

API Request → trace_id: "xyz-123"
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "register_user" (10ms)
  │   └─ DB Query (5ms)
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "enqueue_email" (2ms)
  │   └─ Redis LPUSH (1ms)
  │   └─ trace_id attached to job
  │
  └─ Response (sent in 20ms)

Worker picks up job with trace_id: "xyz-123"
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "process_email" (5000ms)
  │   ├─ Connect to SMTP (100ms)
  │   ├─ Send email (4900ms)
  │   ├─ trace_id: "xyz-123" ← linked to original request!
  │   └─ Mark complete

Logs are now correlated:
  [xyz-123] User registered
  [xyz-123] Email queued
  [xyz-123] Email sent successfully

Complete Async Architecture

API Server (50K req/sec)
  │
  ├─ Fast path: Create DB record (10ms)
  │  └─ Return response to user immediately
  │
  └─ Async path: Enqueue job (2ms)
     └─ Return job_id

Redis Queue
  │
  ├─ Job 1: send_email (5000ms)
  ├─ Job 2: generate_report (30000ms)
  ├─ Job 3: resize_image (2000ms)
  └─ ...

Worker Pool (3 workers)
  │
  ├─ Worker 1: Processing send_email (currently)
  ├─ Worker 2: Processing resize_image (currently)
  └─ Worker 3: Waiting for job

Monitoring:
  Queue length: 150 jobs pending
  Worker utilization: 66% (2/3 busy)
  P95 job latency: 2.3 seconds from enqueue to complete

Real-World Example: User Registration

// Synchronous (old way)
POST /api/register
  → Create user (10ms)
  → Hash password (50ms) ← slow!
  → Send email (5000ms) ← very slow!
  → Return 200 OK (5060ms total)

// Asynchronous (new way)
POST /api/register
  → Create user (10ms)
  → Queue: {type: "hash_password", user_id: 123}
  → Queue: {type: "send_email", email: "..."}
  → Return 200 OK + job_ids (20ms)

User sees response in 20ms instead of 5060ms!
  → 250x faster from user's perspective
  → Password hashing & email send in background

Benefits:
  ✓ Fast response time
  ✓ Better UX (no waiting for slow operations)
  ✓ Graceful degradation (if email service is down, user still created)

Testing: 25+ Test Cases

✓ Job enqueued successfully
✓ Worker picks up job
✓ Job processed successfully
✓ Transient failure triggers retry
✓ Exponential backoff timing correct
✓ Max retries exhausted → DLQ
✓ Trace ID propagated through job
✓ Worker pool processes 3 jobs in parallel
✓ Poison pill (invalid job) logged without blocking
✓ Multiple workers don't process same job
✓ Job priority honored (high jobs first)
✓ Job scheduled_at timestamp honored

Lessons Learned

1. Not everything needs to be synchronous

If user doesn't need the result immediately, make it async.

2. Retry with exponential backoff

Handles transient failures without overwhelming the system.

3. Dead-letter queues are essential

Failed jobs need investigation. Don't silently discard them.

4. Trace IDs propagate through the system

Link async jobs back to original request for debugging.

5. Worker pool sizing matters

3 workers per 10K req/sec is reasonable starting point. Monitor queue length.

Next: Monitoring & Alerting

Now we need visibility into system health:

  • Prometheus metrics collection
  • Grafana dashboards
  • Alert rules (CPU, memory, latency)
  • SLA monitoring (99.99% uptime)
  • Custom business KPIs

    if err == nil {
      return true  // Success!
    }

    if attempts < job.max_retries {
      // Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...
      time.Sleep(time.Duration(backoff) * time.Second)
      backoff *= 2
    }
  }

  return false  // All retries exhausted
}

Component 5: Dead-Letter Queues

Problem: Job fails after all retries, what happens?

Solution: Dead-letter queue (DLQ)

                Normal Queue
                     │
    ┌────────────┬────┴────┬──────────────┐
    │            │         │              │
  Success    Temporary   Permanent      MAX_RETRIES
             Failure     Failure        Exceeded
    │            │         │              │
    ↓            ↓         ↓              ↓
 Delete      Retry      Dead-Letter   Dead-Letter
             (backoff)    Queue         Queue

Process:
1. Job fails permanently
2. Retries exhausted
3. Move to DLQ
4. Alert operator
5. Manual investigation

Later:
6. Fix root cause
7. Reprocess DLQ jobs

Component 6: Distributed Tracing for Async Jobs

Problem: Job fails in background, how do we debug?

Trace ID propagation:

API Request → trace_id: "xyz-123"
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "register_user" (10ms)
  │   └─ DB Query (5ms)
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "enqueue_email" (2ms)
  │   └─ Redis LPUSH (1ms)
  │   └─ trace_id attached to job
  │
  └─ Response (sent in 20ms)

Worker picks up job with trace_id: "xyz-123"
  │
  ├─ SPAN: "process_email" (5000ms)
  │   ├─ Connect to SMTP (100ms)
  │   ├─ Send email (4900ms)
  │   ├─ trace_id: "xyz-123" ← linked to original request!
  │   └─ Mark complete

Logs are now correlated:
  [xyz-123] User registered
  [xyz-123] Email queued
  [xyz-123] Email sent successfully

Complete Async Architecture

API Server (50K req/sec)
  │
  ├─ Fast path: Create DB record (10ms)
  │  └─ Return response to user immediately
  │
  └─ Async path: Enqueue job (2ms)
     └─ Return job_id

Redis Queue
  │
  ├─ Job 1: send_email (5000ms)
  ├─ Job 2: generate_report (30000ms)
  ├─ Job 3: resize_image (2000ms)
  └─ ...

Worker Pool (3 workers)
  │
  ├─ Worker 1: Processing send_email (currently)
  ├─ Worker 2: Processing resize_image (currently)
  └─ Worker 3: Waiting for job

Monitoring:
  Queue length: 150 jobs pending
  Worker utilization: 66% (2/3 busy)
  P95 job latency: 2.3 seconds from enqueue to complete

Real-World Example: User Registration

// Synchronous (old way)
POST /api/register
  → Create user (10ms)
  → Hash password (50ms) ← slow!
  → Send email (5000ms) ← very slow!
  → Return 200 OK (5060ms total)

// Asynchronous (new way)
POST /api/register
  → Create user (10ms)
  → Queue: {type: "hash_password", user_id: 123}
  → Queue: {type: "send_email", email: "..."}
  → Return 200 OK + job_ids (20ms)

User sees response in 20ms instead of 5060ms!
  → 250x faster from user's perspective
  → Password hashing & email send in background

Benefits:
  ✓ Fast response time
  ✓ Better UX (no waiting for slow operations)
  ✓ Graceful degradation (if email service is down, user still created)

Testing: 25+ Test Cases

✓ Job enqueued successfully
✓ Worker picks up job
✓ Job processed successfully
✓ Transient failure triggers retry
✓ Exponential backoff timing correct
✓ Max retries exhausted → DLQ
✓ Trace ID propagated through job
✓ Worker pool processes 3 jobs in parallel
✓ Poison pill (invalid job) logged without blocking
✓ Multiple workers don't process same job
✓ Job priority honored (high jobs first)
✓ Job scheduled_at timestamp honored

Lessons Learned

1. Not everything needs to be synchronous

If user doesn't need the result immediately, make it async.

2. Retry with exponential backoff

Handles transient failures without overwhelming the system.

3. Dead-letter queues are essential

Failed jobs need investigation. Don't silently discard them.

4. Trace IDs propagate through the system

Link async jobs back to original request for debugging.

5. Worker pool sizing matters

3 workers per 10K req/sec is reasonable starting point. Monitor queue length.

Next: Monitoring & Alerting

Now we need visibility into system health:

  • Prometheus metrics collection
  • Grafana dashboards
  • Alert rules (CPU, memory, latency)
  • SLA monitoring (99.99% uptime)
  • Custom business KPIs

You can't fix what you can't see. This post covers monitoring infrastructure: Prometheus metrics collection, Grafana dashboards, alert rules (CPU, memory, latency, throughput), SLA monitoring for 99.99% uptime, and custom business KPIs.

Production systems fail silently. Let's build visibility first.

The Monitoring Problem

Without monitoring:

  • Users report slowness → "It's slow, fix it" (no data)
  • Database fails → You find out from customer complaints (2 hours late)
  • Memory leak → Server crashes at 3 AM (no warning)
  • DDoS attack → Website down, you don't know why

With monitoring:

  • Alert triggers at 95% CPU (before crash)
  • Latency spike detected in seconds
  • Memory trend tracked (leak detected before crash)
  • Request rate spike = DDoS (auto-scale or block)

Component 1: Prometheus Architecture

What is Prometheus? Time-series database for metrics. Scrapes endpoints every 15 seconds, stores data locally.

Application (exposes metrics)
  │
  ├─ GET /metrics
  │   Returns: cpu_usage=0.65, memory_bytes=1024000, requests_total=150000
  │
Prometheus (scraper)
  │
  ├─ Every 15 seconds: scrape /metrics
  ├─ Store data with timestamp: {cpu_usage: 0.65, timestamp: 1711516800}
  ├─ Query interface: localhost:9090
  │
Grafana (visualization)
  │
  ├─ Queries Prometheus every 1 minute
  ├─ Renders graphs
  └─ Shows on dashboard

Key Metrics Types

1. Counter (always increasing)
   - requests_total: 150,000 (can only go up)
   - errors_total: 2,500
   - bytes_sent: 1,024,000

2. Gauge (can go up or down)
   - cpu_usage: 0.65 (65%)
   - memory_bytes: 1,024,000
   - active_connections: 450

3. Histogram (distribution)
   - request_duration: [0.001s, 0.005s, 0.010s, 0.050s, 0.100s, +Inf]
   - Calculates: p50, p95, p99 latencies

4. Summary (similar to histogram)
   - Similar to histogram, older style

Component 2: Instrumentation (Adding Metrics)

Example: Exposing metrics from Go server

import "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"

var (
  requestCounter = prometheus.NewCounterVec(
    prometheus.CounterOpts{Name: "http_requests_total"},
    []string{"method", "endpoint"},
  )

  requestDuration = prometheus.NewHistogramVec(
    prometheus.HistogramOpts{
      Name: "http_request_duration_seconds",
      Buckets: []float64{0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1},
    },
    []string{"method", "endpoint"},
  )
)

// In request handler:
func handleRequest(w, r) {
  start := time.Now()

  // Your logic here
  doWork()

  // Record metrics
  duration := time.Since(start).Seconds()
  requestCounter.WithLabelValues(r.Method, r.URL.Path).Inc()
  requestDuration.WithLabelValues(r.Method, r.URL.Path).Observe(duration)
}

// Expose /metrics endpoint
func init() {
  prometheus.MustRegister(requestCounter)
  prometheus.MustRegister(requestDuration)
  http.Handle("/metrics", promhttp.Handler())
}

Component 3: Grafana Dashboards

Dashboard layout for 50K req/sec system:

┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Requests/sec (time series)          │ Real-time traffic
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ P50 / P95 / P99 Latency             │ Response time percentiles
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ CPU Usage | Memory Usage | Disk I/O  │ Resource utilization
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Database Connections | Cache Hit %   │ Dependency health
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Error Rate (5xx, 4xx)               │ Application health
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Queue Length | Worker Utilization   │ Async processing
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Typical dashboard update: Every 10 seconds (30-second graphs)

Metrics show WHAT happened. Logs show WHY it happened. This post covers structured logging, ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Jaeger distributed tracing, and how to trace requests across 10+ microservices.

A single metric (request failed) means nothing. Logs tell the story.

The Logging Problem

Bad logging practices:

  • Unstructured logs: "Error: connection failed" (no context)
  • No trace ID: Can't correlate related logs from different services
  • Local logs only: SSH into 10 servers to debug (painful)
  • Lost logs on restart: Server crashes, logs gone

Good logging practices:

  • Structured JSON logs: {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, user_id, message}
  • Trace ID propagation: Same ID through entire request lifecycle
  • Centralized logging: All logs in one searchable place
  • Long retention: 30-90 days for investigation

Component 1: Structured Logging (JSON Format)

Bad log (unstructured):

2026-03-27 10:15:32 ERROR User registration failed: connection timeout

Good log (structured JSON):

{
  "timestamp": "2026-03-27T10:15:32.123Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "auth-service",
  "trace_id": "xyz-123",
  "span_id": "span-456",
  "user_id": 789,
  "endpoint": "/api/register",
  "method": "POST",
  "message": "Database connection timeout",
  "error": "connection deadline exceeded",
  "duration_ms": 5000,
  "db_host": "postgres.example.com"
}

1. Parseable (JSON, not free text)

Docker containers are great, but managing 100 containers by hand is nightmare. Kubernetes orchestrates them: auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, and resource management at scale.

Kubernetes makes container orchestration possible at 50K req/sec.

The Kubernetes Problem

Without Kubernetes (manual deployment):

  • CPU spikes → SSH into server, manually scale containers
  • Container crashes → Manually restart (or wait for monitoring alert)
  • Update rollout → Update each server one by one (error-prone)
  • Resource allocation → Overprovisioned to prevent outages

With Kubernetes (automatic):

  • CPU spike → Auto-scale to 10 replicas in 2 minutes
  • Container crashes → Automatically restart
  • Update rollout → Rolling update, automatic rollback if health checks fail
  • Resource allocation → Pack containers efficiently, bin packing

Component 1: Pod (Smallest Deployable Unit)

Pod = one or more containers

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-server
  labels:
    app: api
    version: v1
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "100m"
      limits:
        memory: "512Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5

Key concepts:

- resources.requests: Kubernetes reserves this amount (minimum)
- resources.limits: Container can't exceed this
- livenessProbe: Is container alive? Restart if not
- readinessProbe: Is container ready to serve? (remove from load balancer if not)

Component 2: Deployment (Manage Replicas)

Deployment = Pod template + replica count + update strategy

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3  # Always run 3 copies
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1      # 1 extra pod during update
      maxUnavailable: 0 # Never take down all pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"

Component 3: Service (Network Exposure)

Service = stable endpoint for pod traffic

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP  # Internal only
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
  - port: 80       # Service port
    targetPort: 8080 # Pod port
    protocol: TCP

Service types:

1. ClusterIP (default)
   - Internal only, load balanced across pods
   - Use: Microservice communication

2. NodePort
   - Expose on node's port (30000-32767)
   - Use: Testing, small deployments

3. LoadBalancer
   - Cloud provider's load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP LB)
   - Use: External traffic

4. ExternalName
   - Route to external service (database outside cluster)

Component 4: Ingress (HTTP Routing)

Ingress = HTTP/HTTPS routing rules

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - api.example.com
    secretName: api-tls
  rules:
  - host: api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /v1
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-service
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /v2
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-v2-service
            port:
              number: 80

Component 5: Persistent Volumes (Storage)

StatefulSet for databases (unlike Deployment, preserves identity)

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi

---

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  replicas: 1
  serviceName: postgres
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:13
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: fast-ssd
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi

Component 6: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaling)

Auto-scale replicas based on metrics

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api-deployment
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 50
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 15
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15

Autoscaling behavior:

Current load: 70% CPU (50% target)
→ Scale up by 100% every 15 seconds
→ 3 → 6 → 12 → 25 → 50 (max)

Scale up is fast (reach peak in 60s)
Scale down is slow (stabilization: 5 minutes)
Result: Handles traffic spikes, doesn't oscillate

Component 7: ConfigMap & Secrets

ConfigMap (non-sensitive configuration)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  database_pool_size: "100"
  cache_ttl_seconds: "300"
  log_level: "INFO"

---

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-config

Secret (sensitive data)

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
type: Opaque
data:
  username: dXNlcm5hbWU=  # base64 "username"
  password: cGFzc3dvcmQx  # base64 "password1"

---

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
    env:
    - name: DB_USER
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: username
    - name: DB_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password

Complete K8s Architecture (50K req/sec)

┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Cloud Load Balancer     │ (AWS ELB, GCP LB)
└────────────┬─────────────┘
             │
┌────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Ingress Controller       │ (Nginx)
│  Route to services        │
└────────────┬──────────────┘
             │
┌────────────▼──────────────────────┐
│  Kubernetes Cluster                │
├────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                    │
│  Deployment: api (25 replicas)    │
│  ├─ Pod 1, Pod 2, ... Pod 25      │
│  │  Each: 256Mi mem, 100m CPU     │
│  │                                 │
│  Deployment: worker (5 replicas)   │
│  └─ Pod 1-5 (background jobs)     │
│                                    │
│  StatefulSet: postgres (1 replica) │
│  └─ Pod 1 (database, 100Gi PV)    │
│                                    │
│  HPA: Scales based on CPU/memory   │
│                                    │
└────────────────────────────────────┘

Deployment Workflow

1. Push Docker image
   docker push myregistry/api:v1.2.4

2. Update Deployment manifest
   image: myregistry/api:v1.2.4

3. Apply to cluster
   kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

4. Rolling update happens automatically
   - Spin up 1 new pod (v1.2.4)
   - Health check passes (readiness probe)
   - Drain 1 old pod
   - Repeat until all updated

5. If health checks fail, automatic rollback
   kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-deployment

Real-World Example: Bank API

Cluster configuration:

Deployments:
  ├─ API servers: 10-50 replicas (HPA)
  ├─ Auth service: 5-20 replicas
  └─ Notification workers: 3-10 replicas

StatefulSets:
  └─ PostgreSQL: 1 master + 2 replicas

Services:
  ├─ api-service → API servers
  ├─ auth-service → Auth service

Docker containers are great, but managing 100 containers by hand is nightmare. Kubernetes orchestrates them: auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, and resource management at scale.

Kubernetes makes container orchestration possible at 50K req/sec.

The Kubernetes Problem

Without Kubernetes (manual deployment):

  • CPU spikes → SSH into server, manually scale containers
  • Container crashes → Manually restart (or wait for monitoring alert)
  • Update rollout → Update each server one by one (error-prone)
  • Resource allocation → Overprovisioned to prevent outages

With Kubernetes (automatic):

  • CPU spike → Auto-scale to 10 replicas in 2 minutes
  • Container crashes → Automatically restart
  • Update rollout → Rolling update, automatic rollback if health checks fail
  • Resource allocation → Pack containers efficiently, bin packing

Component 1: Pod (Smallest Deployable Unit)

Pod = one or more containers

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-server
  labels:
    app: api
    version: v1
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "100m"
      limits:
        memory: "512Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5

Key concepts:

- resources.requests: Kubernetes reserves this amount (minimum)
- resources.limits: Container can't exceed this
- livenessProbe: Is container alive? Restart if not
- readinessProbe: Is container ready to serve? (remove from load balancer if not)

Component 2: Deployment (Manage Replicas)

Deployment = Pod template + replica count + update strategy

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3  # Always run 3 copies
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1      # 1 extra pod during update
      maxUnavailable: 0 # Never take down all pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myregistry/api:v1.2.3
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"

Component 3: Service (Network Exposure)

Service = stable endpoint for pod traffic

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP  # Internal only
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
  - port: 80       # Service port
    targetPort: 8080 # Pod port
    protocol: TCP

Service types:

1. ClusterIP (default)
   - Internal only, load balanced across pods
   - Use: Microservice communication

2. NodePort
   - Expose on node's port (30000-32767)
   - Use: Testing, small deployments

3. LoadBalancer
   - Cloud provider's load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP LB)
   - Use: External traffic

4. ExternalName
   - Route to external service (database outside cluster)

Component 4: Ingress (HTTP Routing)

Ingress = HTTP/HTTPS routing rules

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - api.example.com
    secretName: api-tls
  rules:
  - host: api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /v1
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-service
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /v2
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-v2-service
            port:
              number: 80

StatefulSet for databases (unlike Deployment, preserves identity)

apiVersion: v1

metadata:
  name: postgres-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi

---

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  replicas: 1
  serviceName: postgres
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres

        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432

        - name: data

  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: fast-ssd
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi

Component 6: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaling)

Auto-scale replicas based on metrics

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api-deployment
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 50
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 15
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15

Autoscaling behavior:

Current load: 70% CPU (50% target)
→ Scale up by 100% every 15 seconds
→ 3 → 6 → 12 → 25 → 50 (max)

Scale up is fast (reach peak in 60s)
Scale down is slow (stabilization: 5 minutes)
Result: Handles traffic spikes, doesn't oscillate

Manually building Docker images and pushing them is error-prone. CI/CD pipelines automate the entire flow: push code → run tests → build image → deploy to Kubernetes → verify health.

Good CI/CD means you ship code, not artifacts.

The CI/CD Problem

Manual deployment:

  • Git push → Someone runs tests locally (maybe)
  • Build image → Docker build (slow, manual)
  • Push to registry → Docker push (manual)
  • Deploy → kubectl apply (manual, error-prone)
  • Verify → Manual health checks (might skip)

Automated pipeline:

  • Git push → Automatic tests (unit + integration)
  • Tests pass → Automatic image build (cached layers)
  • Image push → Automatic K8s deployment
  • Auto-verify → Health checks, smoke tests
  • Failed test → Block deployment (no bad code shipped)

Component 1: GitHub Actions Workflow

GitHub Actions = serverless CI/CD in your repo

name: Build and Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Set up Go
      uses: actions/setup-go@v2
      with:
        go-version: 1.19

    - name: Run tests
      run: |
        go test ./... -race -v
        go test ./... -bench=. -benchmem

    - name: Run linting
      uses: golangci/golangci-lint-action@v2
      with:
        version: latest

    - name: SAST (security scan)
      uses: securego/gosec@master
      with:
        args: '-no-fail -fmt sarif -out /tmp/gosec-report.sarif ./...'

    - name: Upload SARIF
      uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v1
      with:
        sarif_file: /tmp/gosec-report.sarif

  build:
    needs: test  # Don't build if tests fail
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v1

    - name: Login to Docker Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v1
      with:
        registry: myregistry.azurecr.io
        username: \${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USERNAME }}
        password: \${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v2
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: myregistry.azurecr.io/api:\${{ github.sha }}
        tags: myregistry.azurecr.io/api:latest
        cache-from: type=registry,ref=myregistry.azurecr.io/api:buildcache
        cache-to: type=registry,ref=myregistry.azurecr.io/api:buildcache,mode=max

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Update K8s manifests
      run: |
        sed -i "s/image: .*/image: myregistry.azurecr.io\\/api:\\${{ github.sha }}/g" deployment.yaml

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
        kubectl rollout status deployment/api-deployment

    - name: Health check
      run: |
        for i in {1..10}; do
          status=\$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.example.com/health)
          if [ \$status -eq 200 ]; then
            echo "Health check passed"
            exit 0
          fi
          sleep 10
        done
        echo "Health check failed"
        exit 1

    - name: Smoke tests
      run: |
        curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/test -d '{"test": "data"}'
        # Add more smoke tests here

  rollback:
    if: failure()  # Only run if previous steps failed
    needs: deploy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - name: Rollback deployment
      run: |
        kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-deployment

Component 2: Docker Build Optimization

Multi-stage build (small final image):

FROM golang:1.19 as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o api .

FROM alpine:3.17
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /app/api /app/api
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/app/api"]

Result:

golang:1.19 (1.3GB) → removed after build
alpine:3.17 (7MB) → final image
Final image size: ~50MB (instead of 1.3GB!)
Build cache: Layer-by-layer, reuses unchanged layers

Component 3: Testing Pipeline

Test pyramid (investment of test time):

    /\
   /  \       E2E (10 tests, 2 minutes)
  /────\      Integration (30 tests, 3 minutes)
 /──────\     Unit tests (100+ tests, 30 seconds)

Example test script:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "Running unit tests..."
go test ./... -race -v

echo "Running integration tests..."
docker-compose up -d postgres redis
sleep 5
go test ./tests/integration/... -v
docker-compose down

echo "Running E2E tests..."
kubectl apply -f e2e-test-pod.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/e2e-tests --timeout=300s
kubectl logs job/e2e-tests

echo "All tests passed!"

Component 4: Blue-Green Deployment

Zero-downtime deployment strategy:

Before deployment:
Load Balancer → Blue (v1.2.3, all traffic)
Load Balancer → Green (empty, v1.2.4 ready)

Steps:
1. Deploy to Green (v1.2.4)
2. Run smoke tests on Green
3. Switch Load Balancer to Green
4. Keep Blue running (fallback)
5. Monitor Green for 10 minutes
6. If stable, delete Blue
7. If unstable, switch back to Blue (rollback in 30 seconds)

Component 5: Code Quality Gates

Checks that block deployment:

✓ All tests pass
✓ Code coverage > 80%
✓ No linting errors
✓ No security vulnerabilities (SAST)
✓ No dependency CVEs
✓ Build successful
✓ Health check passes
✓ Smoke tests pass

Any one failure → Block deployment, notify team

  │   ├─ Run unit tests (go test ./...)

  │   │
  │   ├─ Run linting (golangci-lint)
  │   │   └─ If fail: STOP

  │   ├─ SAST scan (gosec)

  │   │
  │   ├─ Build Docker image (docker buildx)
  │   │   └─ Push to registry
  │   │
  │   ├─ Update K8s manifest (sed, update image tag)
  │   │   └─ Apply: kubectl apply
  │   │
  │   ├─ Health check (curl /health)
  │   │   └─ If fail after 5 retries: ROLLBACK
  │   │
  │   ├─ Smoke tests (curl /api/test)
  │   │   └─ If fail: ROLLBACK

Tests block bad code from shipping. Alerts inform the team instantly.

2. Build once, deploy everywhere

Docker image is immutable artifact. Same artifact in dev, staging, prod.

No more "I forgot to run tests" or "forgot to update config".

4. Rollback is your safety net

Problems in production? Rollback in seconds. Investigate later.

5. Monitoring + CI/CD = confidence

You know deployment is working because health checks pass.

How do you go from 10K to 50K req/sec? Profiling, identifying bottlenecks, optimizing one layer at a time, and validating each improvement with benchmarks.

Performance isn't about guessing. It's about measuring, identifying the slowest part, fixing it, and repeating.

The Performance Problem

Starting point: 10K req/sec with high latency

Metrics:
  - Throughput: 10,000 req/sec
  - P99 Latency: 2000ms (bad!)
  - Error rate: 2% (connection timeouts)
  - Database CPU: 95% (maxed out)
  - API CPU: 45% (idle!)

This tells us: bottleneck is the database, not API logic.

Step 1: Bottleneck Identification (Profiling)

Tools:

Go:
  - pprof (CPU, memory, goroutine profiling)
  - trace (execution timeline)

Python:
  - cProfile (function-level CPU)
  - memory_profiler (line-by-line memory)

Node.js:
  - clinic.js (CPU, memory, I/O)
  - node --prof (V8 profiler)

Example: Go pprof

// Add profiling to your binary
import _ "net/http/pprof"

// Run with profiling endpoint
curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=10 > cpu.prof
go tool pprof cpu.prof

(pprof) top10
Showing nodes accounting for 8500ms, 85.00% of 10000ms total
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
    3000ms 30.00% 30.00%     5000ms 50.00% database/sql.Scan
    2000ms 20.00% 50.00%     3500ms 35.00% crypto/sha256.Sum256
    1500ms 15.00% 65.00%     1500ms 15.00% time.Sleep (garbage collection)
    1000ms 10.00% 75.00%     2000ms 20.00% net.Dial
    ...

Findings:

1. database/sql.Scan: 50% of time (connection overhead)
2. SHA-256 hashing: 35% of time (key hashing)
3. Garbage collection: 15% of time (allocations)
4. Network dial: 20% of time (no connection pooling)

Step 2: Fix Connection Pooling (50% improvement)

Problem: New database connection per request = 300ms overhead

Solution: Connection pool

Before:
  Request → Open connection (300ms) → Query (10ms) → Close (20ms) = 330ms
  10K req/sec × 330ms = 3300 seconds = 55 cores needed

After (pool of 100):
  Request → Borrow connection (1ms) → Query (10ms) → Return (1ms) = 12ms
  10K req/sec × 12ms = 120 seconds = 2 cores

Improvement: 330ms → 12ms = 27.5x faster!

Code:

var db *sql.DB
db, err := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)
db.SetMaxOpenConns(100)
db.SetMaxIdleConns(50)
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(time.Hour)

Benchmark result:

Before: 10,000 req/sec, P99=2000ms
After:  25,000 req/sec, P99=500ms

Improvement: 2.5x throughput, 4x latency reduction

Step 3: Replace SHA-256 with FNV-1a (5x improvement)

Problem: SHA-256 is slow (computing 32 bytes when only using 4)

Solution: FNV-1a hash (much faster)

// Before
func hash(key string) uint32 {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(key))
    return binary.BigEndian.Uint32(sum[:4])
}

// After
func hash(key string) uint32 {
    h := fnv.New32a()
    h.Write([]byte(key))
    return h.Sum32()
}

Benchmark:

BenchmarkSHA256-8      500000     2000ns/op
BenchmarkFNV1a-8      5000000      380ns/op

Improvement: 2000ns → 380ns = 5.3x faster

System impact:

Hash operations: 15% of time (from pprof)
15% × 5.3x improvement = 7% overall improvement
Throughput: 25K → 27K req/sec

Step 4: Reduce Garbage Collection (3x improvement)

Problem: Every request allocates new buffers

Solution: sync.Pool (reuse allocations)

var bufPool = sync.Pool{
    New: func() interface{} {
        return make([]byte, 0, 512)
    },
}

func handleRequest(req []byte) {
    buf := bufPool.Get().([]byte)
    defer bufPool.Put(buf[:0])  // Reset and return

    // Use buf instead of allocating new buffer
}

Allocation rate before: 1000MB/sec
Allocation rate after: 100MB/sec (10x reduction)
GC pause time: 50ms → 5ms (10x reduction)

System impact:

GC time: 15% of CPU (from pprof)
Reduction: 15% × (50ms → 5ms) = 5ms per request = 5% improvement
Throughput: 27K → 32K req/sec

Step 5: Query Optimization (10% improvement)

Problem: Database executing inefficient queries

Solution: Add indexes, optimize queries

Query: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = ?
  Before: Full table scan (1M rows checked) = 50ms
  After: Index lookup (20 comparisons) = 0.1ms
  Improvement: 500x faster

Query: SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
  Before: No index (full scan + sort) = 100ms
  After: Composite index (user_id, created_at) = 2ms
  Improvement: 50x faster

System impact:

Database CPU: 95% → 40% (less work)
Query time: 10ms → 2ms average
Throughput: 32K → 40K req/sec

Step 6: Load Balancing & Horizontal Scaling (2x improvement)

Problem: Single API server (CPU limited)

Solution: Run 3 API servers + load balancer

Load Balancer (round-robin)
  ├─ API Server 1 (CPU: 40%)
  ├─ API Server 2 (CPU: 40%)
  └─ API Server 3 (CPU: 40%)

Before: 1 server at 40K req/sec, CPU = 95%
After: 3 servers at ~50K req/sec, CPU = 40% per server

Improvement: 40K → 50K req/sec (25% increase)
Room to grow before hitting CPU limits again

1       Connection pooling    25K/sec     500ms         2.5x
2       FNV-1a hashing        27K/sec     450ms         1.08x
3       sync.Pool buffers     32K/sec     300ms         1.18x
4       Query indexes         40K/sec     100ms         1.25x
5       Load balance (3x)     50K/sec     50ms          1.25x

Total improvement: 10K → 50K req/sec (5x)
Total latency: 2000ms → 50ms (40x)

Lessons Learned

1. Profile first, guess never

Use profiling tools to identify actual bottlenecks, not assumptions.

2. One layer at a time

Fix network layer, then database, then application logic. Identify the slowest part first.

3. Measure everything

Benchmark before/after each change. Some optimizations hurt other metrics.

4. Horizontal scaling beats vertical

3 servers better than 1 massive server (cheaper, fault-tolerant).

5. Diminishing returns

First 5 optimizations get you 90% of the way. Last 10% takes 90% of the effort.

You shipped perfect code. But production still breaks. This post covers common issues, debugging techniques, memory leak detection, deadlock resolution, and post-mortem analysis to prevent future incidents.

Production incidents are inevitable. How you respond determines whether they're learning opportunities or disasters.

The Troubleshooting Problem

When production breaks:

  • Panic mode → No one knows what's happening
  • Blame game → "Is it networking?" "Is it the database?"
  • Band-aid fixes → Restart server, hope it works
  • No root cause analysis → Incident repeats next week

Proper incident response:

  • Triage (determine severity)
  • Restore service (fastest fix, even if temporary)
  • Investigate (root cause analysis)
  • Document (post-mortem)
  • Prevent (permanent fix, tests)

Common Production Issues (Case Studies)

Incident 1: Memory Leak (CPU high, memory grows)

Symptoms:

Timeline:
10:00 - Server starts: Memory = 100MB
10:30 - Memory = 200MB (doubled)
11:00 - Memory = 400MB (still growing)
11:30 - OOM killer → Server crashes (memory limit reached)

Investigation:

1. Take memory profile
   curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap.prof
   go tool pprof heap.prof

2. Analyze top allocators
   (pprof) top10
   Showing nodes accounting for 500MB, 95% of 512MB total
       flat  flat%  sum%    cum   cum%
     200MB 39.06% 39.06%  300MB 58.59% bytes.Buffer.String
     150MB 29.30% 68.36%  200MB 39.06% strings.Builder
     100MB 19.53% 87.89%  150MB 29.30% io.ReadAll

3. Root cause: ReadAll in a loop without cleanup
   for {
     body := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // Allocates, never freed
     process(body)
     // resp.Body never closed!
   }

Fix:

for {
  resp, _ := http.Get(url)
  body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
  process(body)
  resp.Body.Close()  // ← KEY: Close the reader!
}

Incident 2: Database Deadlock (Requests hanging)

Symptoms:

10:15 - API responses normal
10:16 - Requests start timing out (taking 30s)
10:17 - P99 latency = 30,000ms
10:18 - All requests blocked (0 successful)

Investigation:

    needs: test  # Don't build if tests fail

    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v1

    - name: Login to Docker Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v1

Manually building Docker images and pushing them is error-prone. CI/CD pipelines automate the entire flow: push code → run tests → build image → deploy to Kubernetes → verify health.

Good CI/CD means you ship code, not artifacts.

The CI/CD Problem

Manual deployment:

  • Git push → Someone runs tests locally (maybe)
  • Build image → Docker build (slow, manual)
  • Push to registry → Docker push (manual)
  • Deploy → kubectl apply (manual, error-prone)
  • Verify → Manual health checks (might skip)

Automated pipeline:

  • Git push → Automatic tests (unit + integration)
  • Tests pass → Automatic image build (cached layers)
  • Image push → Automatic K8s deployment
  • Auto-verify → Health checks, smoke tests
  • Failed test → Block deployment (no bad code shipped)

Component 1: GitHub Actions Workflow

GitHub Actions = serverless CI/CD in your repo

name: Build and Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Set up Go
      uses: actions/setup-go@v2
      with:
        go-version: 1.19

    - name: Run tests
      run: |
        go test ./... -race -v
        go test ./... -bench=. -benchmem

    - name: Run linting
      uses: golangci/golangci-lint-action@v2
      with:
        version: latest

    - name: SAST (security scan)
      uses: securego/gosec@master
      with:
        args: '-no-fail -fmt sarif -out /tmp/gosec-report.sarif ./...'

    - name: Upload SARIF
      uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v1
      with:
        sarif_file: /tmp/gosec-report.sarif

  build:
    needs: test  # Don't build if tests fail
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v1

    - name: Login to Docker Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v1
      with:
        registry: myregistry.azurecr.io
        username: \${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USERNAME }}
        password: \${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v2
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: myregistry.azurecr.io/api:\${{ github.sha }}
        tags: myregistry.azurecr.io/api:latest
        cache-from: type=registry,ref=myregistry.azurecr.io/api:buildcache
        cache-to: type=registry,ref=myregistry.azurecr.io/api:buildcache,mode=max

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2

    - name: Update K8s manifests
      run: |
        sed -i "s/image: .*/image: myregistry.azurecr.io\\\\/api:${{ github.sha }}/g" deployment.yaml

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
        kubectl rollout status deployment/api-deployment

    - name: Health check
      run: |
        for i in {1..10}; do
          status=\$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.example.com/health)
          if [ \$status -eq 200 ]; then
            echo "Health check passed"
            exit 0
          fi

        done
        echo "Health check failed"
        exit 1

        curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/test -d '{"test": "data"}'

Component 2: Docker Build Optimization

Multi-stage build (small final image):

FROM golang:1.19 as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o api .

FROM alpine:3.17
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /app/api /app/api
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/app/api"]

Result:

golang:1.19 (1.3GB) → removed after build
alpine:3.17 (7MB) → final image
Final image size: ~50MB (instead of 1.3GB!)
Build cache: Layer-by-layer, reuses unchanged layers

Component 3: Testing Pipeline

Test pyramid (investment of test time):

    /\
   /  \       E2E (10 tests, 2 minutes)
  /────\      Integration (30 tests, 3 minutes)
 /──────\     Unit tests (100+ tests, 30 seconds)

Example test script:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "Running unit tests..."
go test ./... -race -v

echo "Running integration tests..."
docker-compose up -d postgres redis
sleep 5
go test ./tests/integration/... -v
docker-compose down

echo "Running E2E tests..."
kubectl apply -f e2e-test-pod.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/e2e-tests --timeout=300s
kubectl logs job/e2e-tests

echo "All tests passed!"

Component 4: Blue-Green Deployment

Zero-downtime deployment strategy:

Before deployment:
Load Balancer → Blue (v1.2.3, all traffic)
Load Balancer → Green (empty, v1.2.4 ready)

Steps:
1. Deploy to Green (v1.2.4)
2. Run smoke tests on Green
3. Switch Load Balancer to Green
4. Keep Blue running (fallback)
5. Monitor Green for 10 minutes
6. If stable, delete Blue
7. If unstable, switch back to Blue (rollback in 30 seconds)

Component 5: Code Quality Gates

Checks that block deployment:

✓ All tests pass
✓ Code coverage > 80%
✓ No linting errors
✓ No security vulnerabilities (SAST)
✓ No dependency CVEs
✓ Build successful
✓ Health check passes
✓ Smoke tests pass

Any one failure → Block deployment, notify team

Complete CI/CD Workflow

Developer pushes code to main branch
  │
  ├─ GitHub Actions triggered
  │   │
  │   ├─ Run unit tests (go test ./...)
  │   │   └─ If fail: STOP, notify developer
  │   │
  │   ├─ Run linting (golangci-lint)
  │   │   └─ If fail: STOP
  │   │
  │   ├─ SAST scan (gosec)
  │   │   └─ If vulnerabilities found: STOP
  │   │
  │   ├─ Build Docker image (docker buildx)
  │   │   └─ Push to registry
  │   │
  │   ├─ Update K8s manifest (sed, update image tag)
  │   │   └─ Apply: kubectl apply
  │   │
  │   ├─ Health check (curl /health)
  │   │   └─ If fail after 5 retries: ROLLBACK
  │   │
  │   ├─ Smoke tests (curl /api/test)
  │   │   └─ If fail: ROLLBACK
  │   │
  │   └─ Success: Code in production (1 hour from commit)

If anything fails at any step:
  - Step 1-3 fail: Developer notified, code not built

  - Deploy fails: Automatic rollback to previous version

Lessons Learned

1. Fail fast, fail loudly

Tests block bad code from shipping. Alerts inform the team instantly.

2. Build once, deploy everywhere

Docker image is immutable artifact. Same artifact in dev, staging, prod.

3. Automation removes human error

No more "I forgot to run tests" or "forgot to update config".

4. Rollback is your safety net

Problems in production? Rollback in seconds. Investigate later.

5. Monitoring + CI/CD = confidence

You know deployment is working because health checks pass.
